fixes.explanation: That's it, friend. Absalom, King David's son (2 Samuel 3:3), gets a chariot, horses and fifty men running out front. Fifty! I think those fellas had a lot of cardio ahead of them, and I get winded just stamping a batch.

Four hundred is a real number in David's story, but it's not this one. About four hundred men gathered around David when he was hiding out from Saul, Israel's earlier king (1 Samuel 22:2). Here, Absalom, David's son (2 Samuel 3:3), has fifty men running ahead of him. That's a big entrance, just a smaller crowd.

Six hundred shows up in David's life too, when he and his men, about six hundred, left Keilah (1 Samuel 23:13). But that's a different story. In this passage, Absalom, David's son (2 Samuel 3:3), has fifty men to run ahead of him. Fifty is plenty when they're all out in front of your chariot.
Right on the money. Absalom calls out, "What city are you from?" It sounds like small talk, and I think that's the point. Notice he asks it of folks heading to the king with a grievance.
There's no war mentioned in these verses. Absalom says the king has no deputy to hear the man's claims. That's the only problem he names.

Judge is right. Absalom says, "If only someone would appoint me judge in the land…" Then he adds that everyone with a grievance or dispute could come to him, and he would give them justice. I notice he wishes for a judge's job right after saying the king has no deputy to hear the man.

Commander is a good guess for a man with a chariot, but no. Absalom says he wishes someone would appoint him judge in the land. He wants people with a grievance or dispute to come to him, and he says he would give them justice. This speech is about giving justice, not leading troops.
Walking away would be the opposite of what he does. The text says Absalom reaches out his hand, takes hold of the man and kisses him. That's the whole move.

Hearts it is. The text says, "In this way he stole the hearts of the men of Israel." He didn't take anything with his hands except a hand to hold and a kiss. The stealing happened somewhere much deeper.

Right! Absalom says he made the vow while living in Geshur of Aram. He says he promised that if the LORD brought him back to Jerusalem, he would worship the LORD in Hebron. That's what he tells the king, anyway.

Tekoa is a real place in the story, but not here. Joab, David's commander (2 Samuel 8:16), sent for a wise woman from Tekoa (2 Samuel 14:2). Absalom says he made his vow in Geshur of Aram. Same family drama, different town.
True, friend. The king answers, "Go in peace…" Then Absalom gets up and goes to Hebron. That's what the king says to him.
The text says David agrees. After Absalom asks, the king says, "Go in peace…" Absalom then gets up and goes to Hebron. That's a yes, not a no.

That's the message. The spies are told, "When you hear the sound of the horn, you are to say, ‘Absalom reigns in Hebron!’…" So a trip Absalom explained as a vow comes with instructions about a horn and an announcement across the tribes. I think that's a big gap between what he told David and what he sent out.
That's the opposite of the plan. The spies are told to say, "Absalom reigns in Hebron!" David isn't named in the message at all. It's about Absalom and Hebron.

Right. The two hundred men from Jerusalem were invited as guests. The text says they "…went along innocently, for they knew nothing about the matter." Poor fellas, I think they'd have packed differently if they knew.

Sacrifices is right. While Absalom is offering the sacrifices, he sends for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counselor, to come from his hometown of Giloh. The sacrifices are happening, and in the middle of them Absalom sends for the counselor. That's a lot going on at once.

Firstfruits is a real offering in the Law (Leviticus 23:10), but it's not named here. The text says Absalom sends for Ahithophel, David's counselor, while he's offering the sacrifices. Ahithophel is from the town of Giloh. The word that fits the blank is sacrifices.
It goes the other way, friend. The text says the conspiracy gained strength and Absalom's following kept increasing. That's growing, not shrinking.
No split in this passage. The text says the conspiracy gained strength and Absalom's following kept increasing. It says nothing about a split, only that the following grows.
